faq.a: Rise in oxygen tension and fall in prostaglandin E2 cause smooth‑muscle constriction, functionally closing the shunt within 24‑48 h.
faq.q: Why does the ductus arteriosus close after birth?

faq.a: Dry, stimulate, and if no respirations within 30 s, begin positive‑pressure ventilation with a bag‑valve‑mask.
faq.q: What is the first step if a newborn is not breathing?

faq.a: Use skin‑to‑skin contact, pre‑warmed blankets, and a warm environment (≥25 °C); monitor temperature every 15 min.
faq.q: How can I keep a newborn warm without a radiant warmer?

exam: A term infant has a heart rate of 90 bpm after drying and stimulation — what is your next action? — Initiate positive‑pressure ventilation because HR <100 bpm indicates inadequate oxygenation.

A preterm baby shows grunting, nasal flaring, and chest retractions at 30 min of life — which condition is most likely and why? — Respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency; early onset and prematurity are key clues.
Why is a low Apgar score not always synonymous with poor outcome? — It reflects immediate adaptation; many infants improve with simple supportive measures, so follow‑up is essential.
In a setting without pulse oximetry, how would you assess oxygenation? — Observe colour, chest movement, and use capillary refill; consider arterial blood gas if available.

A newborn born to a mother with malaria presents with fever and lethargy at 12 h — what investigations and management steps are indicated? — Perform rapid malaria test; start parenteral artesunate if positive, give supportive fluids and monitor glucose.

What are the physiological reasons for the rapid fall in pulmonary vascular resistance after the first breath? — Lung aeration increases oxygen tension and expands alveoli, reducing vascular resistance and increasing left‑atrial pressure, which closes fetal shunts.
How does hypothermia worsen metabolic transition? — Cold stress increases catecholamine release, raises oxygen consumption, and accelerates glycogen depletion, leading to hypoglycaemia and acidosis.
When is it appropriate to give supplemental oxygen to a newborn with SpO₂ 92 % at 5 min? — Reserve oxygen for SpO₂ <90 %; unnecessary oxygen can cause oxidative injury, especially in preterms.
ai.title: Neonatal Physiologic Transition
related: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: The first hours after birth involve rapid changes in respiration, circulation, temperature, and metabolism as the newborn adapts to extra‑uterine life. Understanding normal physiology helps recognise pathological failure of transition, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Fetal circulation: ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale, ductus venosus
Key physiologic milestones: first breath, lung aeration, rise in systemic vascular resistance
sections.p: At birth the infant must switch from placental gas exchange to pulmonary breathing, close fetal shunts, maintain temperature, and regulate glucose. Most changes occur within the first 24 h.

t.b: Assesses immediate adaptation; low score (<7) signals need for resuscitation and close monitoring
Detects hypoxaemia; SpO₂ <90 % at 5 min suggests respiratory distress

b: Lung aeration → fall in pulmonary vascular resistance → increased left‑atrial pressure closes foramen ovale
Increase in systemic vascular resistance → closure of ductus arteriosus (functional by 24‑48 h)
Brown‑fat thermogenesis + skin‑to‑air heat loss; aim >36.5 °C core
Glucose homeostasis; newborns rely on glycogen stores, need feeding within 1 h
sections.p: Four inter‑related domains drive successful transition: respiratory, circulatory, thermal, and metabolic.

t.b: Confirms lung expansion; ‘ground‑glass’ pattern suggests RDS, normal aeration shows successful transition
Detects hypoglycaemia; <2.6 mmol/L warrants feeding or IV dextrose

b: Premature lung surfactant deficiency → respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
Perinatal infection (e.g., sepsis, malaria) → poor lung compliance and metabolic derangement
Maternal hypertension → delayed lung fluid clearance
sections.p: Failure of transition can present as respiratory distress, persistent pulmonary hypertension, hypothermia, or hypoglycaemia. In low‑resource hospitals, common contributors include prematurity, infection, maternal malaria, and maternal HIV‑related complications.

t.b: Identifies sepsis; positive result guides antibiotic choice
Detects congenital malaria; positive test requires antimalarial therapy

b: Always assess breathing effort, heart rate, colour, and tone within the first minute.
If heart rate <100 bpm after drying and stimulation, start positive‑pressure ventilation.
Temperature <36.5 °C in the first hour is an emergency; initiate warming measures.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of physiology with bedside assessment and prioritisation of interventions.

t.b: Detects crackles or absent breath sounds; absent sounds suggest severe RDS or airway obstruction
Prolonged >3 s indicates poor perfusion, may need fluid bolus

b: Assuming mild tachypnoea is normal; persistent >60 breaths/min with grunting warrants investigation.
Delaying feeding >2 h; early feeding prevents hypoglycaemia.
Relying solely on visual assessment of colour; use pulse oximetry when possible.
sections.p: Pitfalls often stem from misinterpreting normal adaptation as pathology or missing subtle signs of failure.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent heart rate <60 bpm despite ventilation
SpO₂ <85 % after 10 min of effective breathing
